Beyond Action Prediction: Learning Search-Free Planning in Latent Space

Guanchen Du1,  Jinhao Du2,  Yanpeng Sun3, Shan Zhang4,  Na Zhao3,  Zechao Li1 1Nanjing University of Science and Technology  2University of Oxford 3Singapore University of Technology and Design  4Adelaide University Project page: https://hijp.demohub.live
Abstract

Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9–16.5× planning speedup over search-based planning.

1 Introduction

Latent world models encode high-dimensional visual observations into compact latent representations and learn an action-conditioned latent predictor from offline trajectories, providing a foundation for visual planning and control (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). However, planning with these models typically requires optimizers such as CEM (Rubinstein, 1999) or MPPI (Williams et al., 2017) to repeatedly generate and evaluate candidate action sequences at each replanning step, which requires substantial test-time computation (Pinneri et al., 2021). Learning a direct mapping from the current state and goal to actions therefore provides a promising alternative for improving the planning efficiency of latent world models (Sun et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026).

Recent work has introduced action supervision to improve latent world models’ control capabilities. SMWM learns action-relevant representations through inverse dynamics supervision (Ivashkov et al., 2026), while Delta-JEPA (Zhang et al., 2026) recovers actions from latent state differences, encouraging representations to retain action-related state changes. GC-IDM (Nguyen et al., 2026) further learns a goal-conditioned action mapping on frozen representations, while INTACT (Sun et al., 2026)incorporates local and future-goal action supervision into end-to-end training, supporting search-free recursive control. These approaches demonstrate the value of action supervision for goal-conditioned control. However, accurate action prediction alone does not necessarily provide all the supervision needed for search-free planning.

We identify two aspects that remain underconstrained. First, goal-conditioned action supervision should not only train an inverse model to predict actions, but also help shape visual representations to capture how actions relate current states to future goals. Offline trajectories naturally contain such relations at multiple temporal scales: for the same current state and demonstrated action, different future observations define goals at different temporal horizons. However, existing training schemes (Sun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a) exploit only a subset of these relations, for example by conditioning action prediction on a fixed future endpoint. More generally, treating the goal representation only as a conditioning target limits the extent to which action supervision can shape goal-side visual features. Second, accurate action prediction alone does not ensure that the predicted action induces the correct transition under the learned latent predictor. The inverse dynamics model and the latent predictor model are typically supervised separately, with the latter conditioned on demonstrated actions (Ivashkov et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). During search-free rollout planning, however, these two mappings are applied sequentially: the inverse dynamics model predicts an action toward the goal, and the latent predictor model uses this predicted action to advance the latent state for subsequent action generation. The resulting inverse-to-predictor composition is therefore directly involved in planning, yet is not explicitly constrained by separate action and latent prediction objectives. This motivates extending action supervision beyond action prediction itself, using it both to shape goal-conditioned representations and to couple predicted actions with their induced latent transitions.

Based on this principle, we propose Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), which jointly trains a visual encoder, a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics model, and a latent predictor model end-to-end. HIJP relabels future observations within each trajectory window as goals, exposing the inverse objective to diverse state–goal relations across temporal horizons. Gradients are retained through the goal representations, allowing inverse-action supervision to directly shape the visual features used for goal-conditioned action prediction. We further feed the predicted actions into the latent predictor and align the resulting successor latents with the encodings of the next observations. This action-transition consistency objective jointly updates the inverse and predictor models, directly coupling action generation with its induced latent transition. In this way, HIJP trains the same inverse-to-predictor mapping that is repeatedly applied during planning. At test time, the inverse dynamics module and latent predictor model alternate to generate multi-step action sequences, which are executed through closed-loop replanning without online action search.

We evaluate HIJP on four visual control tasks under four configurations of goal temporal offsets and execution budgets. HIJP achieves an overall success rate of 86.8%86.8\%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.94.9 percentage points. Ablations on hindsight goal sampling, training objectives, and gradient routing examine how goal-side representation learning and inverse - predictor coupling contribute to control performance. Beyond success rates, we also evaluate efficiency and the temporal smoothness of executed actions. With matched numbers of replanning calls, HIJP achieves a 1.91.9–16.5×16.5\times planning speedup over LeWM. Under the most challenging setting, its executed actions exhibit lower jerk than those produced by CEM using the same representations, indicating smoother executed controls.

2 Related work

Latent World Models

Latent world models learn action-conditioned changes in representation space to support goal-directed planning from offline visual trajectories. Existing approaches span pretrained visual features, end-to-end representation learning, and large-scale video pretraining (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Assran et al., 2025; Bo et al., 2026). Systematic studies further investigate how architectures, training objectives, and planning algorithms affect control performance (Terver et al., 2025). Gao and Xu (2026) reduce forward-rollout costs through parallel prediction conditioned on action prefixes. Wang et al. (2026a) use inverse dynamics and goal-conditioned action supervision to improve planning representations, while retaining CEM for control. HIJP builds on latent forward dynamics and focuses on learning a goal-conditioned action mapping that can be directly deployed for control.

Inverse Dynamics and Goal-Conditioned Action Learning

Inverse dynamics and action-supervised objectives encourage representations to retain action-relevant state changes. These objectives can also be combined with physical-state alignment to improve representations for control (Ivashkov et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Hindsight learning relabels achieved states along trajectories as goals, providing supervision for goal-conditioned policies and inverse dynamics learning (Andrychowicz et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019). Goal-conditioned action-sequence prediction has also been used for visual planning (Paster et al., 2020). Related theoretical studies analyze the benefits of inverse dynamics through bias–variance trade-offs and learning-problem complexity (Schäfer et al., 2026; Morin et al., 2026). Within latent world models, GC-IDM(Nguyen et al., 2026) learns a goal- and horizon-conditioned action mapping on frozen representations, while INTACT (Sun et al., 2026) jointly learns local and goal-conditioned action prediction to support search-free recursive control. HIJP follows this direction by enriching supervision through future-goal relabeling within trajectory windows.

Learned and Amortized Planning

Planning computation can be shifted to training by learning action priors, latent subgoals, or plan-update rules (Wang et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026; Masip et al., 2026; Sommer and Schilling, 2026; Tang et al., 2025). Another line of work first predicts future states or generates state trajectories and then recovers actions through inverse dynamics (Tian et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026; Ajay et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2026). Rakhimov et al. (2026) jointly train state and action flows, allowing a single model to support multiple control inference modes. HIJP alternates goal-conditioned action prediction with forward latent-state prediction to construct multi-step plans without online action search.

Consistency and Goal-Aware Planning Objectives

Consistency objectives also connect model prediction with planning. Seo et al. (2026) incorporate action-recovery errors from predicted transitions into the online planning cost, while Bai and Xiong (2026) combine temporal-progress learning with multi-step rollout consistency supervision. HIJP focuses on the composed output of the goal-conditioned action module and the forward model. During training, it aligns the successor latent state predicted under the generated action with the encoding of the next observation in the recorded trajectory, allowing state-prediction errors to supervise action learning directly.

3 Methodology

Our goal is to extend action supervision beyond action prediction itself, such that it also shapes goal-conditioned visual representations and constrains the latent transitions induced by predicted actions. HIJP jointly learns a visual encoder fθf_{\theta}, a latent predictor model gϕg_{\phi}, and a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics model hξh_{\xi}. Given offline visual trajectories, the inverse dynamics model learns to predict actions toward future goals, while the predictor predicts action-conditioned latent transitions. We couple these components during training to supervise the local inverse-to-predictor composition repeatedly used in search-free planning. Figure 1 provides an overview.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒟={τ(i)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{\tau^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} be a dataset of trajectories, where

τ=(o0,𝐚0,o1,…,𝐚T−1,oT).\tau=(o_{0},\mathbf{a}_{0},o_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{T-1},o_{T}). (1)

Here oto_{t} is a visual observation and 𝐚t\mathbf{a}_{t} is the action taken at time tt. Given a current observation oto_{t} and a goal observation ogo_{g}, the task is to produce actions that reach the goal within a fixed interaction budget. Training uses recorded observations and actions, with future observations in each trajectory serving as hindsight goals, where reward annotations are not required. Our planning procedure repeatedly composes two mappings. An inverse model predicts an action from the current latent state and goal latent state, and a latent predictor model predicts the latent state induced by that action. This composition motivates training the models together: action prediction must identify a useful action, while the resulting transition must agree with the observed dynamics.

3.2 Latent World Model

Following the prior work (Maes et al., 2026), a visual encoder fθ:𝒪→ℝdf_{\theta}:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} maps observations to latent states zt=fθ​(ot)z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t}), and an action-conditioned latent predictor model gϕg_{\phi} predicts the next latent state from a causal context of latent states and actions:

z^t+1=gϕ(zt−m+1:t,at−m+1:t),zt+1=fθ(ot+1).\hat{z}_{t+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(z_{t-m+1:t},a_{t-m+1:t}\right),\qquad z_{t+1}=f_{\theta}(o_{t+1}). (2)

We train the latent prediction model on demonstrated transitions using

ℒpred=MSE⁡(z^t+1,zt+1).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{z}_{t+1},z_{t+1}). (3)

We also apply ℒsigreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sigreg}} to the encoded observations in each training window to discourage representational collapse. We use a ViT-Tiny encoder trained from scratch and a causal Transformer model with context length m=3m=3. An action encoder supplies the latent prediction model with action embeddings. Architecture and optimization details are given in Appendix  B. The same model also accepts the shorter context used for the one-step consistency objective below.

The latent prediction model learns how demonstrated actions transform latent states. Our next objective is complementary: to learn how actions can be inferred from current and goal representations, while allowing this action supervision to shape the representations themselves.

3.3 Hindsight-conditioned Inverse Dynamics

A trajectory contains multiple valid future goals for a given observation. To expose these relations during training, we sample a window of WW observations, an anchor ii and a future offset κ\kappa:

i∼Unif{0,…,W−2},κ∣i∼Unif{1,…,W−1−i}.i\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,W-2\},\qquad\kappa\mid i\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,W-1-i\}. (4)

Each sampled pair therefore defines a goal-conditioned action-learning problem at a potentially different temporal horizon. Unlike using only the endpoint of a trajectory window, this construction exposes the inverse objective to diverse relations between current observations and future goals using the same offline data. The observation at i+κi+\kappa becomes the hindsight goal. The goal-conditioned inverse model predicts the demonstrated action at the anchor:

a^i=hξ​(zi,zi+κ),ℒinv=MAE⁡(a^i,ai).\hat{a}_{i}=h_{\xi}(z_{i},z_{i+\kappa}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}}=\operatorname{MAE}(\hat{a}_{i},a_{i}). (5)

Although the sampled goal may be several steps ahead, the target is the immediate action aia_{i}, not the intervening action sequence. Each training window therefore supplies action supervision under goals at different temporal offsets.

Gradients from ℒinv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}} flow through both ziz_{i} and zi+κz_{i+\kappa}. Consequently, the inverse objective trains not only hξh_{\xi}, but also the visual features used to represent the current observation and the future goal. We implement hξh_{\xi} as an MLP operating on the concatenated latent pair.

3.4 Action Transition Consistency

The inverse model can predict an action close to the demonstrated action without ensuring that this prediction produces the observed transition under the learned predictor model. This distinction matters at planning time, where the model receives predicted rather than demonstrated actions. We therefore pass the predicted action through gϕg_{\phi}:

z~i+1=gϕ​(zi,a^i),a^i=hξ​(zi,zi+κ),\tilde{z}_{i+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(z_{i},\hat{a}_{i}\right),\qquad\hat{a}_{i}=h_{\xi}(z_{i},z_{i+\kappa}), (6)

and align the result with the encoded one-step successor:

ℒcyc=MSE⁡(z~i+1,sg⁡[zi+1]),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=\operatorname{MSE}\!\left(\tilde{z}_{i+1},\operatorname{sg}[z_{i+1}]\right), (7)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. This objective uses the one-step successor zi+1z_{i+1} even when the hindsight goal zi+κz_{i+\kappa} is farther away. It allows LcycL_{\mathrm{cyc}} to update the inverse head, action encoder, latent prediction model, and the anchor-side visual representation. Thus, the consistency objective does not merely use the prediction model to provide an error signal to the inverse dynamics model; it jointly adapts action generation and the latent predictor around their composed prediction. This directly supervises the inverse-to-latent predictor transition that is repeatedly composed during search-free planning.

3.5 Joint Objective and Search-free Planning

Joint training. The full training objective combines latent prediction, representation regularization, hindsight-conditioned action prediction, and action-transition consistency:

ℒ=ℒpred+λreg​ℒsigreg+λinv​ℒinv+λcyc​ℒcyc.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}+\lambda_{\text{reg}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigreg}}+\lambda_{\text{inv}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}}+\lambda_{\text{cyc}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}}. (8)

All components are optimized jointly, and all terms are averaged over their corresponding batch, temporal, sampled-pair, and feature dimensions before weighting. For all tasks, the loss weights are set to λreg=0.09\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=0.09, λinv=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}=1.0, and λcyc=0.05\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.05 for TwoRoom and 0.100.10 for the remaining tasks.

Search-free planning. At planning time, we use the inverse dynamics model and latent prediction models in the same order in which they are coupled during training. At each replanning point, the latest observation and fixed goal observation are encoded as zt=fθ​(ot)z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t}) and zg=fθ​(og)z_{g}=f_{\theta}(o_{g}). Starting from z^0=zt\hat{z}_{0}=z_{t}, we construct an HH-step plan by alternating goal-conditioned action prediction and latent prediction:

aj=hξ(z^j,zg),z^j+1=gϕ(z^ℓj:j,aℓj:j),ℓj=max(0,j−m+1),j=0,…,H−1.a_{j}=h_{\xi}(\hat{z}_{j},z_{g}),\qquad\hat{z}_{j+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(\hat{z}_{\ell_{j}:j},a_{\ell_{j}:j}\right),\quad\ell_{j}=\max(0,j-m+1),\quad j=0,\ldots,H-1. (9)

The inverse model therefore predicts each action from the current imagined state and fixed goal, while the latent prediction model advances the imagined state under that predicted action. We use H=5H=5, execute the resulting action sequence, observe the environment again, and repeat the procedure in a receding-horizon manner. Each replanning call requires only one inverse-to-latent prediction rollout, without sampling or iteratively refining candidate action sequences.

4 Experiments

We conduct experiments on four tasks to answer the following key questions: (i) whether our method achieves strong goal-reaching performance, particularly for long-horizon goals; (ii) how much inference speed is gained by replacing the CEM search at test time with a single amortized rollout; (iii) how hindsight goal relabeling, inverse-action supervision, gradient routing, and predicted-action transition consistency contribute to control performance; and (iv) how HIJP and CEM differ in latent-space goal progress and executed-action smoothness.

4.1 Experiment setup

Benchmarks and Tasks

We evaluate on four goal-conditioned control benchmarks with distinct dynamics: TwoRoom (22D navigation), Reacher (DMControl reacher), PushT (planar pushing), and OGCube (OGBench cube manipulation). All tasks use 224×224224{\times}224 RGB observations, continuous actions, and observation-specified goals. The dataset information is provided in Appendix A. We use the offline datasets released by LeWM (Maes et al., 2026) without modification. To vary difficulty, we set each goal to the environment state K∈{10,25,50,75}K\in\{10,25,50,75\} steps ahead of the start and assign a corresponding interaction budget B∈{25,50,100,100}B\in\{25,50,100,100\}, defining the easy, default (LeWM’s(Maes et al., 2026) original goal-setting horizon and interaction budget), hard, and extreme tiers, respectively. All methods are evaluated in the original simulator on the same start–goal instances, with 5050 episodes per task–tier combination. An episode counts as successful only when the simulator’s native success condition is met; we use no latent-space distance threshold. We report success rate as the primary metric and planning time for the efficiency study, with additional details in Appendix A.2.

Baselines

We compare against eight baselines: Random, GCBC (Ghosh et al., 2021), DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025), PLDM (Sobal et al., 2025), LeWM (Maes et al., 2026), SMWM (Ivashkov et al., 2026), delta-JEPA (Zhang et al., 2026) and INTACT(Sun et al., 2026). Random provides a chance-level reference; GCBC and INTACT provide direct goal-conditioned controllers, with INTACT representing the closest end-to-end search-free baseline. The remaining methods are latent world-model planners that rely on CEM- or MPPI-based search at test time. All learned methods are trained on the same offline datasets and evaluated under the same protocol. All CEM-based comparisons use the shared search and execution protocol specified in Appendix A.3.

Implementation Details

HIJP combines a latent world model with an amortized inverse head trained end-to-end. At planning time, it produces an H=5H=5 step latent plan with a single amortized rollout, executes the corresponding actions in a receding-horizon manner, and then replans from the latest observation. Unlike the CEM-based world-model baselines, HIJP uses no test-time search. Architecture and optimization details are provided in Appendix B.

4.2 Planning Performance

We first examine how HIJP’s goal-reaching performance compares with the baselines. As detailed in Section 4.1, we test HIJP and all baseline methods on each task-tier combination, using 50 episodes per pair, and report success rates in Table  1.

Table 1 shows that HIJP achieves the highest overall success rate of 86.8%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.9 percentage points. The gains are most pronounced in challenging manipulation settings. On PushT, HIJP achieves 66% and 42% success in the hard and extreme tiers, respectively, outperforming the best baseline in each tier by 8 and 14 percentage points. On OGCube, it maintains 96% success in both tiers, with corresponding gains of 26 and 10 percentage points. On TwoRoom and Reacher, HIJP remains competitive, ranking second in average success on both tasks. The stronger gains on manipulation are consistent with our design to extend action supervision beyond action prediction itself, shaping goal-conditioned visual representations and constraining the latent transitions induced by predicted actions. We examine the contributions of these two design choices through the ablations in Section 4.4.

4.3 Planning Efficiency

To assess planning efficiency, we compare HIJP with LeWM, a CEM-based world-model planner, under matched numbers of replanning calls. Following Section 4.1, we report total wall-clock planning time for each task–tier combination, with all episodes processed as a single vectorized batch on an RTX 4090 (Table 2).

The result shows that HIJP reduces planning time across all evaluated settings, achieving 1.91.9–16.5×16.5\times speedups over LeWM under matched replanning counts. The average speedups are 6.2×6.2\times, 7.1×7.1\times, 15.0×15.0\times, and 2.8×2.8\times on TwoRoom, Reacher, PushT, and OGCube, respectively. Together with the results in Table 1, these findings show that HIJP achieves substantial planning speedups over LeWM while attaining higher average success rates on all four tasks.

4.4 Ablations

To systematically evaluate the contribution of each component, we conduct ablation studies on the training objectives, gradient propagation, hindsight goal relabeling, and the test-time planner. For the training objectives, we remove one term at a time from Eq. 8: the inverse loss ℒinv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}}, the transition-consistency loss ℒcyc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}, and the SIGReg regularizer ℒsigreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sigreg}}.

We further evaluate two gradient-related variants. In sg⁡[zg]\operatorname{sg}[z_{g}], we stop gradients through the goal representation zgz_{g}. In the frozen-gϕg_{\phi} variant, we retain the latent predictor gϕg_{\phi} in the forward computation but block parameter updates from ℒ​cyc\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{cyc}} while retaining those from ℒ​pred\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{pred}}. To evaluate the contribution of hindsight goal relabeling, we introduce a fixed-goal variant that always uses the latent representation of the final observation in each training window as the goal. Specifically, we sample an anchor step tt uniformly from {0,…,T−2}\{0,\ldots,T-2\}, set zg=zT−1z_{g}=z_{T-1}, and predict the one-step action ata_{t} from (zt,zg)(z_{t},z_{g}).

For the planner ablation, we keep the fully trained representation fixed and replace our amortized rollout with CEM search, thereby isolating the effect of the planning mechanism. All other settings follow Section 4.1. We report results on Reacher, PushT, and OGCube in Table 3. We exclude TwoRoom because all variants achieve near-100% success rates on this task. Furthermore, we examine sensitivity to the inverse and transition-consistency loss weights in Appendix C.

The results show that removing ℒinv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}} causes the largest overall decline, reducing average success from 82.5% to 45.7%. Removing SIGReg also reduces average success substantially, to 47.0%, with near-collapse on Reacher. These results support the importance of action supervision and representation regularization for HIJP’s control performance. The two goal-supervision ablations examine different parts of our design choice. Restricting goals to the final observation of each window reduces average success to 71.7%, while stopping gradients through zgz_{g} reduces it to 78.5%. This supports using multiple future observations as goals and allowing action-related gradients to shape goal representations.

The action consistency ablations examine the contribution of the transition-consistency objective. Removing ℒcyc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}} lowers average success to 76.0%, with the clearest decreases on Reacher and PushT and little change on OGCube. Blocking predictor updates from ℒcyc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}} lowers average success to 78.3%, primarily affecting Reacher. These results support the transition-consistency objective and its updates to the latent predictor, with gains varying across tasks. Finally, replacing the inverse-guided rollout with CEM reduces average success to 69.3% under the matched evaluation protocol, supporting the effectiveness of HIJP’s learned planning mechanism.

4.5 Latent-Space Progress Analysis

HIJP shows its largest gains on long-horizon goals. We next examine how the latent distance to the goal evolves during execution. We compare HIJP, its CEM ablation (Section 4.4), and LeWM. The CEM ablation shares HIJP’s learned representation and replaces HIJP’s amortized inverse-guided rollout with CEM search, isolating the contribution of the planner. On the extreme tier (K=75K{=}75), we execute all methods in the original simulator on the same start–goal instances, following each method’s replanning schedule, and track the normalized latent distance to the goal, dt=∥zt−zg∥/∥z0−zg∥d_{t}=\lVert z_{t}-z_{g}\rVert/\lVert z_{0}-z_{g}\rVert, where ztz_{t} and zgz_{g} are the encoded observation and goal. After an episode succeeds, we hold its last recorded distance constant for the remaining steps. Figure 2 reports the mean and pointwise 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 2 shows that HIJP reaches a lower final normalized latent distance than its CEM ablation on all four tasks. On PushT, the methods exhibit similar initial progress, but HIJP continues to reduce the distance later in the episode as CEM largely plateaus. On TwoRoom and OGCube, HIJP reaches a lower plateau, while on Reacher it exhibits fewer fluctuations after the initial decrease. Compared with its CEM ablation, HIJP’s executed trajectories end closer to the goal in the shared latent representation.

4.6 Smoothness of Executed Actions

We additionally evaluate the temporal smoothness of executed actions. We quantify this with action jerk, the mean ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the second finite difference of the executed action sequence, 1T−2​∑t∥𝐚t−2​𝐚t−1+𝐚t−2∥2\tfrac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{a}_{t}-2\mathbf{a}_{t-1}+\mathbf{a}_{t-2}\rVert_{2} (lower is smoother), following the convention of Nguyen et al. (2026). To attribute any difference to the planner rather than the representation, we compare HIJP against its CEM ablation, which shares the same learned representation and differs only in the planning rule, and include LeWM as a reference. Table 4 reports the extreme tier (K=75K{=}75); the metric definition and full per-tier results are in Appendix D.

The results show that HIJP produces smoother executed actions across all four tasks, with action jerk 14.714.7–26.4×26.4\times lower than its CEM ablation and 15.215.2–24.5×24.5\times lower than LeWM. These results indicate that HIJP’s amortized rollout improves the temporal smoothness of executed controls in addition to its goal-reaching performance and planning efficiency.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework for goal-conditioned visual control. HIJP samples future observations as hindsight goals to enrich inverse-dynamics supervision and allows training gradients to update goal representations. It further feeds predicted actions into a latent predictor model and constrains the resulting latent transitions through a consistency objective. At planning time, the inverse and latent predictor models alternate to construct multi-step action plans without online search. Across four visual control tasks and multiple evaluation configurations, HIJP achieves the highest aggregate goal-reaching performance among the evaluated methods while reducing planning time compared to a search-based world-model planner. Under the most challenging setting, its executed actions are also smoother than those produced by CEM using the same representations. Together, these results suggest that aligning goal-conditioned action learning with the latent transitions used during planning provides an effective route toward efficient, search-free visual control.

6 Limitations

Our evaluation focuses on tasks with a limited temporal span, using fixed planning horizons and replanning schedules. Extending HIJP to substantially longer-horizon tasks remains an important direction. Future work will explore hierarchical subgoal generation, adaptive planning horizons, and dynamic replanning schedules. These extensions aim to decompose longer tasks into shorter goal-conditioned segments and adapt planning and execution intervals to the requirements of each segment.

Appendix

Appendix A Dataset Details and Protocol

We evaluate on four continuous-control benchmarks: Tworoom, Reacher, PushT, and OGBench-Cube (hereafter OGCube), which together span 22D navigation, low-dimensional continuous control, planar object pushing, and robotic cube manipulation; Figure 3 shows a representative trajectory from each. We do not collect any trajectories ourselves: we reuse the full-scale offline datasets released by LeWM (Maes et al., 2026) without modification.

A.1 Datasets

The four datasets are gathered under different behavior policies: a goal-directed navigation policy for Tworoom, a near-uniform random policy for Reacher, and expert policies for PushT and OGCube. This heterogeneity is directly visible in their action distributions (Figure 4): Reacher actions are essentially uniform over [−1,1][-1,1], Tworoom actions saturate at the ±1\pm 1 boundaries, whereas PushT and OGCube produce concentrated, structured actions.

Each dataset is stored as a single HDF5 file under a shared schema: RGB observations pixels of shape (N,224,224,3)(N,224,224,3) in uint8, a continuous action array of shape (N,A)(N,A), and per-episode boundaries encoded by ep_offset and ep_len, so that a sampled window never straddles two episodes. Table 5 summarizes the resulting statistics.

Observations and actions.

All observations are 224×224224\times 224 RGB frames, which we feed to the encoder at full resolution. The action space is a 22D command for Tworoom, Reacher, and PushT, and a 55D vector (end-effector pose and gripper) for OGCube. Reacher and OGCube episodes have a fixed length of 201201 steps, whereas Tworoom and PushT episodes vary in length because they terminate upon task completion.

Action normalization.

Before training, every non-pixel input—the actions, and (where used) proprioception and state—is standardized per dimension by its dataset statistics, i.e., a z-score transform to zero mean and unit variance, applied identically to all four tasks. Figure 4 plots the corresponding raw (pre-normalization) action distributions, which differ markedly across tasks because of their different behavior policies.

Training samples and monitoring split.

Following the data-loading and window-level splitting procedure of the LeWM implementation (Maes et al., 2026), we enumerate all valid windows within each trajectory and randomly assign 90% to training and 10% to validation. Each window contains WW observations sampled at intervals of kk raw environment steps, together with aligned action chunks. The loader requires W​kWk consecutive raw time-step records, while the first and last sampled observations are separated by (W−1)​k(W-1)k environment steps. We replace NaN action entries with zeros during training rather than dropping the window.

A.2 Evaluation Protocol

We follow the dataset-based evaluation procedure of the LeWM implementation (Maes et al., 2026). For each evaluation episode, we sample a start state from an offline trajectory and define the goal as the environment state KK steps ahead (at index start+K\texttt{start}+K). The agent acts for at most BB steps. We count an episode as successful only if the simulator reports task completion within this budget Table 6; latent-space distance is not used to determine success.

By varying the goal offset KK and the step budget BB, we obtain four difficulty tiers (Table 7; Figure 5), ranging from easy (K=10K{=}10) to extreme (K=75K{=}75): a larger KK yields a longer-horizon goal. The extreme tier is the most challenging setting and is where our method attains its largest margin over the baselines.

A.3 CEM Planning Protocol

CEM plays several roles in our experiments. It is used as the test-time optimizer for the CEM-based world-model baselines, as the computational reference in the planning-efficiency experiment, and as a controlled planner ablation in which HIJP’s amortized action generation is replaced by search over the same learned representation and forward dynamics. We therefore use one shared CEM configuration throughout all experiments.

At every replanning point, CEM maintains a factorized Gaussian distribution over action sequences of length H=5H=5 model steps. Each model-level action contains a chunk of k=5k=5 environment actions, so every candidate sequence covers H​k=25Hk=25 environment steps. The sampling distribution is initialized with zero mean and sampling scale 1.01.0.

At each optimization iteration, CEM samples N=300N=300 candidate action sequences and rolls each candidate forward through the corresponding latent dynamics model. Candidates are ranked by the squared distance between their terminal predicted latent and the encoded goal,

Jgoal(𝐚0:H−1)=‖z^H(𝐚0:H−1)−zg‖22.J_{\mathrm{goal}}(\mathbf{a}_{0:H-1})=\left\|\hat{z}_{H}(\mathbf{a}_{0:H-1})-z_{g}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (10)

The best 3030 candidates are retained as elites and are used to refit the sampling mean and scale. This procedure is repeated for I=30I=30 iterations. Consequently, every CEM replanning call evaluates

N​I=300×30=9,000NI=300\times 30=9{,}000 (11)

candidate action sequences. Since every sequence contains H=5H=5 latent transitions, this corresponds to approximately

N​I​H=300×30×5=45,000NIH=300\times 30\times 5=45{,}000 (12)

latent transition predictions per environment and replanning call. These operations are evaluated in parallel on the GPU; therefore, the sequence count should not be interpreted as an equivalent wall-clock slowdown.

All CEM comparisons use the same planning horizon, action chunking, interaction budget, and replanning cadence as HIJP. Both planners generate H=5H=5 model-level actions and execute R=5R=5 model steps, equivalent to R​k=25Rk=25 environment steps, before observing the environment and replanning. Under the interaction budgets B∈{25,50,100,100}B\in\{25,50,100,100\}, the maximum numbers of replanning calls are therefore 11, 22, 44, and 44 for the easy, default, hard, and extreme tiers, respectively.

For the main LeWM baseline, CEM searches using LeWM’s own encoder and forward model. In the controlled CEM ablation, it instead searches using HIJP’s encoder and forward model while completely disabling the inverse-dynamics action generator. This controlled comparison changes only the test-time planning mechanism and therefore isolates the effect of amortized inverse-guided planning.

Appendix B Implementation Details

This appendix provides a concrete instantiation of the method. We first specify the temporal discretization and the architecture of each component, then describe the training procedure and test-time planning protocol. Unless stated otherwise, the architecture and temporal settings are shared across all four tasks.

B.1 Temporal Discretization and Data Flow

The environments expose atomic actions us∈ℝdau_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} at raw environment step ss. The world model operates at a coarser temporal resolution by grouping kk consecutive atomic actions into one model-level action chunk, 𝐚t=(ut​k,ut​k+1,…,ut​k+k−1)∈ℝk​da.\mathbf{a}_{t}=\left(u_{tk},u_{tk+1},\ldots,u_{tk+k-1}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{kd_{a}}.

We use k=5k=5 for every task. Consequently, one transition in the learned latent dynamics corresponds to five raw environment steps. The raw action dimension is da=2d_{a}=2 for Tworoom, Reacher, and PushT, and da=5d_{a}=5 for OGCube. The effective model-level action dimension is therefore d𝐚=k​da∈{10,25}d_{\mathbf{a}}=kd_{a}\in\{10,25\}.

A training sample contains WW temporally subsampled observations, together with their aligned model-level action chunks. k=5k=5 raw environment steps separate consecutive observations. Thus, the first and final observations in a window are separated by (W−1)​k(W-1)k raw environment steps.

Before being passed to the model, images are converted to floating-point, normalized using ImageNet statistics, and resized to 224×224224\times 224. Following the LeWM preprocessing procedure, continuous actions are standardized per dimension using statistics computed from the training dataset. At execution time, predicted action chunks are mapped back to the environment action space using the inverse transformation.

B.2 Architecture

The implementation contains a visual encoder fθf_{\theta}, an action encoder ψω\psi_{\omega}, a latent predictor gϕg_{\phi}, and a hindsight-conditioned inverse-dynamics head hξh_{\xi}. The action encoder is absorbed into the notation of gϕg_{\phi} in the main text and is made explicit here.

Visual encoder fθf_{\theta}.

We instantiate fθf_{\theta} as a ViT-Tiny(Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) trained from scratch, without a pretrained backbone or an external visual representation. It contains 1212 Transformer layers, 33 attention heads, and a hidden width of 192192. Each 224×224224\times 224 observation is divided into patches of size 14×1414\times 14. We take the final[CLS] token and pass it through a projection MLP →→192192\!\rightarrow\!2048\!\rightarrow\!192. Batch normalization is applied at the hidden layer of the projection head. The resulting vector is the latent representation zt=fθ​(ot)∈ℝ192z_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{192}.

Action encoder ψω\psi_{\omega}.

The flattened action chunk 𝐚t∈ℝd𝐚\mathbf{a}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathbf{a}}} is embedded in two stages. A pointwise linear projection, implemented as a 1×11\times 1 one-dimensional convolution, first maps d𝐚→10d_{\mathbf{a}}\!\rightarrow\!10. A two-layer MLP then maps →→19210\!\rightarrow\!768\!\rightarrow\!192, with a SiLU activation between the two linear layers. This produces an action embedding with the same width as the visual latent, eta=ψω​(𝐚t)∈ℝ192.e_{t}^{a}=\psi_{\omega}(\mathbf{a}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{192}.

latent predictor gϕg_{\phi}.

The predictor is a six-layer autoregressive Transformer with causal self-attention. It operates at width 192192, uses 1616 attention heads with head dimension 6464, an MLP width of 20482048, attention and MLP dropout of 0.10.1, and learned positional embeddings. The predictor receives a sequence of latent tokens and a time-aligned sequence of action embeddings. Actions condition every Transformer block through AdaLN-Zero(Peebles and Xie, 2023). In particular, each action embedding produces the shift, scale, and residual-gating parameters for both the attention and feed-forward sublayers; the modulation layer is initialized to zero.

The predictor uses at most the m=3m=3 most recent latent-action pairs. For a context ending at time tt, its last output is interpreted as the prediction of the next latent,z^t+1=gϕ(zt−m+1:t,ψω(𝐚t−m+1:t)),\hat{z}_{t+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(z_{t-m+1:t},\psi_{\omega}(\mathbf{a}_{t-m+1:t})\right),where the context is shortened near the beginning of a sequence. The Transformer output is mapped to the latent space by a second projection MLP →→192192\!\rightarrow\!2048\!\rightarrow\!192 with batch normalization.

Inverse-dynamics head hξh_{\xi}.

The inverse head receives the concatenation of a current latent and a future goal latent,

hξ:ℝ2​d→ℝd𝐚,𝐚^i=hξ​(zi,zi+κ).h_{\xi}:\mathbb{R}^{2d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathbf{a}}},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i}=h_{\xi}(z_{i},z_{i+\kappa}). (13)

It consists of three hidden layers of width 512512. Each hidden layer applies a linear transformation, LayerNorm, and GELU activation. A final linear layer maps to the model-level action dimension d𝐚d_{\mathbf{a}}.

B.3 Training

All four modules are optimized jointly. Training combines next-latent prediction, anti-collapse representation regularization, hindsight-conditioned inverse dynamics, and action transition consistency.

latent prediction loss.

Although every sampled window contains W=16W=16 model steps, the prediction term uses a causal context of length m=3m=3. Specifically, the predictor consumes z0:m−1z_{0:m-1} and the corresponding action embeddings and predicts the shifted latent sequence z1:mz_{1:m}. Because causal attention is used, the output at position tt only depends on positions up to tt. Denoting the three predicted latents by z^1:m\hat{z}_{1:m}, we compute

ℒpred=1B​m​d​∑b=1B∑t=0m−1‖z^t+1(b)−zt+1(b)‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{Bmd}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{t=0}^{m-1}\left\|\hat{z}_{t+1}^{(b)}-z_{t+1}^{(b)}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (14)

The target latent in this term remains attached to the computational graph, for which we do not employ a momentum target encoder.

Anti-collapse regularization.

We apply the Sketch Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025) to the latents from all WW frames, including frames that are not used by Equation 14. SIGReg measures the discrepancy between random one-dimensional projections of the latent distribution and a standard Gaussian reference distribution. We use 1717 integration knots and 10241024 random projections. Applying this objective over the complete window increases the number and temporal diversity of latent samples contributing to the regularizer.

Hindsight-conditioned inverse dynamics.

For each training window, we independently sample NaN_{a} anchor–goal pairs. For the nn-th pair, the anchor is sampled uniformly from all positions with an available successor,

in∼Unif⁡{0,…,W−2}.i_{n}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,W-2\}. (15)

Conditioned on ini_{n}, we sample a future offset uniformly from the remaining part of the window,

κn∼Unif⁡{1,…,W−1−in}.\kappa_{n}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,W-1-i_{n}\}. (16)

The resulting goal index is in+κni_{n}+\kappa_{n}. Sampling is performed independently for each pair and each element of the minibatch, so anchors may repeat. This procedure exposes the inverse head to goal conditions at multiple temporal distances while requiring no rewards or task labels.

For every sampled pair, the inverse head predicts the demonstrated action chunk executed at the anchor,

𝐚^in=hξ​(zin,zin+κn).\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i_{n}}=h_{\xi}(z_{i_{n}},z_{i_{n}+\kappa_{n}}). (17)

Importantly, the target is the immediate action chunk 𝐚in\mathbf{a}_{i_{n}}, not the sequence of actions between the anchor and the sampled goal. The inverse loss is the element-wise mean absolute error

ℒinv=1B​Na​d𝐚​∑b=1B∑n=1Na‖𝐚^in(b)−𝐚in(b)‖1.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}}=\frac{1}{BN_{a}d_{\mathbf{a}}}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{a}}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i_{n}}^{(b)}-\mathbf{a}_{i_{n}}^{(b)}\right\|_{1}. (18)

Action transition consistency loss.

The action consistency term couples the inverse head to the learned latent prediction. For each hindsight pair, we embed the predicted action and perform a single predictor step from the anchor latent,

z~in+1=gϕ​(zin,ψω​(𝐚^in)).\tilde{z}_{i_{n}+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(z_{i_{n}},\psi_{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{i_{n}})\right). (19)

We then regress the prediction toward the actual next latent using

ℒcyc=1B​Na​d​∑b=1B∑n=1Na‖z~in+1(b)−sg⁡[zin+1(b)]‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}=\frac{1}{BN_{a}d}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{a}}\left\|\tilde{z}_{i_{n}+1}^{(b)}-\operatorname{sg}\!\left[z_{i_{n}+1}^{(b)}\right]\right\|_{2}^{2}, (20)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. Gradients from this loss update hξh_{\xi}, ψω\psi_{\omega}, gϕg_{\phi}, and fθf_{\theta}, as well as the anchor-side representation through zinz_{i_{n}}, while the next-latent target is detached. The single-step context used by this term is supported by the same autoregressive predictor used for the length-mm forward objective.

Joint objective.

The complete objective is

ℒ=ℒpred+λreg​ℒsigreg+λinv​ℒinv+λcyc​ℒcyc.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sigreg}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inv}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}}. (21)

All terms are averaged over the batch and their corresponding temporal, anchor, action, or latent dimensions before the weights are applied.

Optimization.

We use a single AdamW optimizer for fθf_{\theta}, ψω\psi_{\omega}, gϕg_{\phi}, and hξh_{\xi}, with weight decay 10−310^{-3}. Training uses bf16 mixed precision and a global gradient-norm clipping threshold of 1.01.0. The learning rate follows a linear-warmup cosine-decay schedule, starting from zero. With ten training epochs, the configured warmup is rounded to one epoch, followed by cosine decay to zero. Training and validation use the LeWM-based window-level split described in the dataset appendix A, with a 90%/10% ratio and random seed 30723072.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete training procedure, and Table 10 reports the task-specific training parameters.

B.4 Planning and Receding-Horizon Execution

At each replanning point, the current observation and target observation are encoded as

z0=fθ​(ot),zg=fθ​(og).z_{0}=f_{\theta}(o_{t}),\qquad z_{g}=f_{\theta}(o_{g}). (22)

Starting from z0z_{0}, we construct an HH-step action sequence through the autoregressive latent rollout introduced in the main text. At rollout step jj, the inverse head first predicts the action chunk that is consistent with moving from the current imagined latent toward the goal latent,

𝐚j=hξ​(zj,zg).\mathbf{a}_{j}=h_{\xi}(z_{j},z_{g}). (23)

The action chunk is embedded and passed to the latent predictor, which advances the imagined state,

zj+1=gϕ(zmax⁡(0,j−m+1):j,ψω(𝐚max⁡(0,j−m+1):j)).z_{j+1}=g_{\phi}\!\left(z_{\max(0,j-m+1):j},\psi_{\omega}(\mathbf{a}_{\max(0,j-m+1):j})\right). (24)

The available context grows from one to mm latent-action pairs during the first rollout steps and is subsequently truncated to the most recent m=3m=3 pairs. Thus, constructing an HH-step plan requires HH evaluations of the inverse head and HH autoregressive evaluations of the latent predictor. No population of candidate action sequences or iterative test-time action optimization is required.

We use H=5H=5 model steps for every task. Since each model-level action contains k=5k=5 atomic actions, one predicted plan covers H​k=25Hk=25 raw environment steps. The controller operates in a receding-horizon loop with execution stride R=5R=5 model steps. It therefore executes the complete predicted action sequence, re-encodes the resulting observation, and constructs a new plan. The target observation remains unchanged within an episode but is encoded together with the current observation at each replanning point. Execution terminates when the task-specific success condition is satisfied, or the allotted budget of raw environment steps is exhausted. Algorithm 2 gives the complete procedure.

Table 11 collects the planning settings shared across the four tasks. Keeping these settings unchanged ensures that differences across tasks do not arise from task-specific planning budgets or model-rollout depths.

Appendix C Loss Weight Ablation

To examine the sensitivity of HIJP to the weighting coefficients of its training objectives, we conduct ablations on the inverse dynamics loss weight λinv\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}} and the cycle-consistency loss weight λcyc\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}.

Specifically, we vary λinv∈{0,0.1,1.0,2.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}\in\{0,0.1,1.0,2.0\} while fixing λcyc=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.1, and vary λcyc∈{0,0.01,0.1,0.2}\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}\in\{0,0.01,0.1,0.2\} while fixing λinv=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}=1.0. We train a separate model for each weight setting and evaluate the resulting checkpoint using the same evaluation protocol as in the main experiments. All training and evaluation settings follow Section 4.1. We report the results on Reacher, PushT, and OGCube in Table 12. We omit TwoRoom because its performance is already saturated under our evaluation protocol, with near 100% success rates, making it uninformative for distinguishing different loss-weight choices.

The default setting, λinv=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}}=1.0 and λcyc=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.1, achieves the highest overall average success rate of 82.5%. Increasing λinv\lambda_{\mathrm{inv}} to 2.0 improves performance on PushT and matches the default performance on OGCube, but reduces performance on Reacher, resulting in a slightly lower overall average of 81.8%. Similarly, decreasing λcyc\lambda_{\mathrm{cyc}} to 0.01 or increasing it to 0.2 yields overall averages of 81.2% and 78.0%, respectively. These results indicate that the default weights provide the best overall balance across the three evaluated environments.

Appendix D Action Smoothness Experiment

This appendix provides the complete evaluation protocol, metric definition, and per-tier results for the action-smoothness study in Section 4.6. We evaluate HIJP, its CEM ablation, and LeWM on the four domains described in Appendix A.

For each domain and difficulty tier, all methods are evaluated closed-loop on the same set of start–goal instances. Instance sampling depends only on the dataset, random seed, goal offset, and number of evaluation episodes, and is therefore independent of the evaluated method. We use 50 episodes per task with random seed 42. The four difficulty tiers are defined by the goal-offset and step-budget pairs (K,B)(K,B) listed in Table 7. Each rollout is allowed to run for the corresponding step budget, and we record the action executed at every environment step.

HIJP directly executes the amortized plan produced by its inverse-guided controller and performs no test-time search. The CEM ablation uses the same learned representation and predictive model as HIJP, but replaces inverse-guided action generation with CEM planning. LeWM, which performs CEM planning over its own forward model, is included as an additional reference. All methods use the same control frequency and normalized action space.

If an episode reaches its goal before exhausting the step budget, we truncate its action sequence at the first success step and compute smoothness only over the executed prefix. This avoids either rewarding or penalizing post-success idling and measures the controls actually required to complete the task. Unsuccessful episodes contribute their full budget-length action sequences.

Let a1:T=(a1,…,aT)a_{1:T}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{T}) denote the executed action sequence of an episode. We define action jerk as the mean ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the discrete second difference:

Jerk(a1:T)=1T−2∑t=3T‖at−2at−1+at−2‖2.\operatorname{Jerk}(a_{1:T})=\frac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t=3}^{T}\left\lVert a_{t}-2a_{t-1}+a_{t-2}\right\rVert_{2}. (25)

Lower values indicate smoother controls. A temporally constant or linearly varying action sequence has zero second difference, whereas oscillatory or abruptly changing commands produce a large value.

For each method, environment, and difficulty tier, we compute Eq.  25 independently for every episode and report the mean across episodes. Let J¯m\overline{J}_{m} denote this episode-averaged jerk for method mm. We additionally report

RCEM=J¯CEMJ¯HIJP,RLeWM=J¯LeWMJ¯HIJP.R_{\mathrm{CEM}}=\frac{\overline{J}_{\mathrm{CEM}}}{\overline{J}_{\mathrm{HIJP}}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{LeWM}}=\frac{\overline{J}_{\mathrm{LeWM}}}{\overline{J}_{\mathrm{HIJP}}}. (26)

A ratio greater than one indicates that HIJP produces smoother actions than the corresponding CEM-based planner. Because all methods are evaluated in the same normalized action space, their jerk values are directly comparable.

Table 13 reports the results across all four difficulty tiers. HIJP consistently achieves lower action jerk than both its CEM ablation and LeWM. On the extreme tier (K=75K=75), the CEM ablation produces 14.7×14.7\times–26.4×26.4\times higher jerk than HIJP, despite sharing the same learned representation and predictive model. This controlled comparison shows that the smoothness advantage primarily arises from HIJP’s amortized inverse-guided planning rather than from a difference in learned representations. LeWM exhibits a similar level of jerk to the CEM ablation, suggesting that independently optimizing successive plans with CEM can introduce substantial temporal discontinuities into the executed controls.

Appendix E Visualizing Planned Trajectories

For each environment, we run our planner (Algorithm 2) from a start observation toward a goal observation and record the resulting trajectory. Figures 6–9 visualize these rollouts as pixel-space filmstrips.

Each figure corresponds to one environment and contains four difficulty tiers: Easy, Default, Hard, and Extreme. The tiers are defined by goal offsets of 1010, 2525, 5050, and 7575 environment steps, with corresponding planning budgets of 2525, 5050, 100100, and 100100 steps, respectively. For each tier, we show one rollout using 1616 frames sampled uniformly over its execution, from 0%0\% to 100%100\%, and arrange them in two rows of eight frames. The goal observation appears separately on the right, outlined in red. The label beside each tier indicates whether the rollout reaches the goal within the planning budget.
